title: Grigsby v. United States
articleTitle: Grigsby v. United States: Boilerplate Work-for-Hire and Confidentiality Clauses as a Bar to the Research Credit
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, affirming the United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana
subject: Funded Research Exclusion — Substantial Rights and Payment Contingency
summary: Grigsby v. United States, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), is a key federal R&D tax credit case for construction contractors claiming Section 41 credits. The Fifth Circuit affirmed denial of Cajun Industries' $1.34 million claim because the taxpayers identified no qualifying business component and all four projects were funded research under § 41(d)(4)(H).

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in United States v. Grigsby (commonly cited as Grigsby v. United States), 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), affirming United States v. Grigsby, Civil Action No. 3:19-cv-00596-BAJ-SDJ (M.D. La. Oct. 19, 2022), represents a watershed precedent in federal research and development (R&D) tax credit jurisprudence under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (26 U.S.C. § 41). Authored by Circuit Judge Patrick E. Higginbotham on behalf of a unanimous appellate panel that included Circuit Judges Jerry E. Smith and Jennifer Walker Elrod, the ruling provides an uncompromising blueprint for how federal courts scrutinize retrofitted R&D tax credit claims, particularly within the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) sector. The Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment in favor of the United States, holding that the taxpayer's claimed credits failed on two independent, dispositive grounds: first, a procedural and substantive failure to establish a viable "business component" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2); and second, complete disqualification under the "funded research" exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation (26 C.F.R.) § 1.41-4A(d).
Factual and Procedural History of the Claim

The dispute originated from the operations of Cajun Industries, LLC ("Cajun"), a Baton Rouge, Louisiana-based heavy civil construction contractor taxed as an S corporation under Subchapter S of the Internal Revenue Code. During the relevant period, Cajun provided construction services throughout the Gulf Coast region, engaging in more than one hundred construction projects during the period in question and contracting with hundreds of private and public clients throughout the Gulf South. Throughout its prior corporate history, Cajun had never claimed the Qualified Research Tax Credit (QRTC) on its originally filed federal income tax returns.

In 2015, Cajun engaged a national tax consulting firm, alliantgroup LP, to conduct a retroactive study evaluating whether the company could amend prior tax returns to claim Section 41 research credits for the 2011 through 2016 tax years. Utilizing a sample of 105 projects from Cajun's 2012 tax year, the consulting firm determined that Cajun was entitled to claim more than $1.3 million in additional research credits. Acting on this study, Cajun filed an amended Form 1120S (U.S. Income Tax Return for an S Corporation) for its fiscal tax year ending September 30, 2013, claiming an R&D tax credit of $1,341,420. Because S corporations operate as pass-through entities for federal income tax purposes, the claimed credit flowed through to Cajun's shareholders on a pro rata basis. Leonard L. Grigsby, who held a 73 percent ownership interest in Cajun, received a Schedule K-1 allocation of $979,237 of the claimed research credit.

Leonard Grigsby and his spouse, Barbara F. Grigsby, subsequently filed an amended 2013 joint individual federal income tax return (Form 1040X), claiming a flow-through research credit of $954,527. This credit reduced their reported 2013 federal income tax liability and generated a claimed tax overpayment of $576,756. On September 15, 2017, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disbursed a refund check to the Grigsbys totaling $671,071.38, which encompassed the $576,756 principal overpayment plus $73,663.38 in statutory overpayment interest (these two amounts, together $650,419.38, are collectively defined in the litigation as the "Contested Refund"), plus an additional refund of $20,652.00 that was not at issue in the case.

On August 13, 2019, the IRS issued a letter advising the Grigsbys that Cajun Industries, LLC & Subsidiaries was not entitled to the Section 41 research credit claimed for the 2013 tax year, that the resulting refund should not have been allowed, and that the disbursement constituted an erroneous refund. The letter demanded repayment and warned that, absent repayment, the IRS would recommend that an action be commenced in District Court to recover the erroneous refund as permitted by 26 U.S.C. §§ 6532(b) and 7405; on September 11, 2019, the United States initiated an erroneous refund recovery suit in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 7405.

To manage the scope of discovery and adjudication across Cajun's extensive construction portfolio, the Government and the taxpayers stipulated to resolve Cajun's entitlement to the 2013 research credit by evaluating four representative construction projects. The first project was the Methanex Project (Project 13-020), a capped subcontract executed with Jacobs Field Services North America, Inc. ("Jacobs") in 2012 to perform site preparation and civil construction services for the relocation of a methanol production facility from Chile to Geismar, Louisiana, for ultimate owner Methanex USA. The second project was the Chevron Project (Project 12-051), a capped (not-to-exceed) contract with Chevron Products Company (as stipulated by the parties and described by the District Court, although the Fifth Circuit's opinion characterizes it as a fixed-price contract) to execute refinery expansion construction work at Chevron's Pascagoula Refinery in Pascagoula, Mississippi. The third project was the Claiborne Project (Project 12-001), a fixed-price federal procurement contract with the United States Army Corps of Engineers to construct an underground flood-control box culvert canal in New Orleans, Louisiana. The fourth project was the East Bank Project (Project 12-023), a fixed-price municipal contract with the Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans to perform flood-protection construction work.

body.text: Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

In the United States, tax credits are strictly a matter of legislative grace and are narrowly construed against the taxpayer claiming the benefit. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer may claim a credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over a statutory base amount. For expenses to qualify as QREs—whether claimed as in-house research wages, supplies, or contract research expenses—the underlying activities must satisfy the four-part statutory definition of "qualified research" set forth in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1).

First, under the Section 174 Test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the research expenditures must be eligible to be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174, meaning they must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. Second, under the Technological in Nature Test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is "technological in nature," which requires that the process of experimentation fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component Test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2), the application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved "business component" of the taxpayer. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B), a business component is exhaustively defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Crucially, § 41(d)(2)(A) mandates that the four-part test be applied separately to each business component of the taxpayer, and § 41(d)(2)(C) ("Special rule for production processes") dictates that any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component must be treated as a separate business component rather than as part of the business component being produced. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all (defined by Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more) of the research activities measured on a cost or time basis must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose relating to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality.

Even where a taxpayer satisfies all four affirmative tests of § 41(d)(1) and maintains contemporaneous substantiation records in "sufficiently usable form and detail" as required by 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d), the claim remains subject to the statutory exclusions of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4). Foremost among these exclusions for government and commercial contractors is the "funded research" exclusion of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), which bars any research "to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)."

The implementing regulations at 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d) (applied via cross-reference in § 1.41-4(c)(9)) and the "mirror image" customer rules in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e) establish a strict two-prong conjunctive standard designed to prevent double-claiming and ensure that only the party bearing genuine financial risk and retaining commercial exploitation rights receives the tax subsidy. Under § 1.41-4A(d)(1), all agreements—not merely formal research contracts—entered into between the researcher and third parties must be examined in determining the extent to which the research is funded. Research performed under contract is treated as unfunded (and thus eligible for the credit) only if the taxpayer proves both that payment is contingent on the success of the research and that the taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research. Under the payment contingency prong of 26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-4A(d)(1) and 1.41-2(e)(2), amounts payable under the agreement must be contingent on the success of the research and therefore considered to be paid for the product or result of the research rather than for the performance of the research services themselves. Under the substantial rights prong of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3), the taxpayer performing the research must retain substantial rights to use or exploit the research results. If the agreement confers exclusive exploitation rights on the customer, or divests the researcher of the right to use the research results in future projects without paying the customer for that right, the researcher retains no substantial rights and the research is disqualified as funded.
Summary of the Final Holding

On October 19, 2022, Judge Brian A. Jackson of the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana granted the Government's motion for summary judgment in full, ordering the Grigsbys to return the Contested Refund. On November 13, 2023, the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The appellate panel held that the IRS's disallowance letter carried the established presumption of correctness, placing on the Grigsbys the burden of producing evidence to rebut that presumption and substantiate every element of the claimed § 41 credit (and held, alternatively, that the Government had in any event met its own summary judgment burden of production). The court concluded that the Grigsbys failed to establish any viable business component because their mid-litigation pivot from claiming "products" in verified interrogatories to claiming "construction processes" at summary judgment violated Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (FRCP) 26(e) and was properly excluded under FRCP 37(c)(1); moreover, even on the merits, the taxpayers failed to identify any specific new or improved process beyond vague references to standard engineering analyses. Independently, the Fifth Circuit held that all four representative projects constituted excluded "funded research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H): Cajun assigned away all substantial rights in the Methanex, Chevron, and Claiborne contracts through boilerplate work-for-hire, confidentiality, and Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) title clauses, and Cajun bore no payment contingency risk in the East Bank contract because its payment terms expressly provided that Cajun's payments constituted full compensation for all loss, damages, or risks connected with the nature of the work or any obstructions or difficulties encountered, and because Cajun was compensated under the contract for the very labor and wages it claimed as research expenses.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

The total disallowance of Cajun's $1.34 million credit claim in Grigsby did not stem from a single isolated oversight; rather, it resulted from a cascading series of procedural, evidentiary, technical, and contractual failures that systematically undermined every pillar of the taxpayer's case. Examining the causal mechanics of these failures reveals how federal courts enforce both procedural litigation rules and substantive tax law to dismantle retrospective credit studies that lack contemporaneous technical and contractual foundations.
Allocation of the Burden of Proof and the Presumption of Correctness in Erroneous Refund Litigation

A threshold legal error committed by the taxpayers on appeal was attempting to shift the evidentiary burden onto the United States at the summary judgment stage. The Grigsbys contended that the District Court erred in granting summary judgment because the Government allegedly failed to prove an absence of genuine factual disputes and relied on an IRS determination that, as counsel argued at oral argument, did not result from an administrative proceeding (a position for which the Fifth Circuit found no supporting authority, noting that there is no prescribed form for a deficiency notice).

The Fifth Circuit dismantled this argument by reaffirming the foundational tax litigation principle articulated in Carson v. United States, 560 F.2d 693 (5th Cir. 1977), and Sealy Power, Ltd. v. Commissioner, 46 F.3d 382, 386 (5th Cir. 1995). Under Fifth Circuit precedent, a determination of deficiency or disallowance issued by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue is vested with a formal "presumption of correctness." Quoting Portillo v. Commissioner, 932 F.2d 1128, 1133 (5th Cir. 1991), Judge Higginbotham observed that while the tax collector's presumption of correctness possesses "a herculean muscularity of Goliathlike reach" that can only be struck at its Achilles' heel when a court finds "no muscles, no tendons, no ligaments of fact," the IRS's August 13, 2019 letter met the low threshold for the presumption because it advised the taxpayers that the IRS had determined a deficiency existed for a particular year and provided the information necessary to compute it. The letter recounted the refund amounts, explained that the $576,756 refund was solely due to information reported on the Grigsbys' amended return (itself based on Cajun's amended Form 1120S), and stated that because the IRS determined that Cajun Industries, LLC & Subsidiaries was not entitled to the research credit claimed, the resulting refund should not have been allowed and was erroneous.

Once the presumption attached, the burden shifted to the Grigsbys to produce evidence refuting the IRS's determination; the Fifth Circuit added that even without the presumption, the Government met its summary judgment burden of production under FRCP 56 by submitting approximately forty exhibits (including contract excerpts, the 2013 amended return, and corporate representative depositions from parties to all four projects), so the Grigsbys were required to come forward with specific, competent evidence, consistent with the recordkeeping requirement of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d), to create a genuine dispute. The Grigsbys' vague and conclusory assertions, which failed to identify even one new or improved construction process, could not overcome the presumption of correctness. This procedural dynamic carries profound second-order implications for taxpayers: even when the IRS initially processes an amended return and disburses a refund check, a subsequent disallowance letter can carry a presumption of correctness in an erroneous refund suit under 26 U.S.C. § 7405; although the United States bears the ultimate burden of proving that some amount was erroneously refunded (United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672, 675 (5th Cir. 2009)), the taxpayer must produce evidence substantiating the claimed credit and, as the Fifth Circuit put it, must ultimately prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the Commissioner's determination was erroneous.
The Business Component Defect: Statutory Separation of Products and Processes and FRCP Rule 37(c)(1) Preclusion

The most devastating procedural and statutory failure in Grigsby occurred at the threshold "business component" step of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2). Under § 41(d)(2)(B), a taxpayer must identify whether the alleged research is intended to develop a new or improved product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention. In the construction industry, claiming the physical structure delivered to the client (such as a refinery, methanol plant, or floodwall) as a "product" business component is fraught with peril: the contractor rarely holds the unique site-specific real property improvement for future sale, lease, or license in its own trade or business, and the physical design specifications of the structure are typically furnished by the owner's third-party architect-engineer. Consequently, sophisticated AEC taxpayers must frame their business components as new or improved construction processes or engineering techniques used by the contractor in its trade or business.

During formal fact discovery, however, the Grigsbys submitted verified interrogatory responses explicitly stating under oath that Cajun had developed a new "product" on each of the four representative projects—described by the Fifth Circuit as two oil refineries and two flood control systems (the District Court relied on the taxpayers' verified supplemental interrogatory responses of November 17, 2021). When the United States, relying on those responses, moved for summary judgment arguing that these four products did not qualify as business components of Cajun, the Grigsbys changed course. In their brief opposing summary judgment—and without ever supplementing their verified interrogatory responses as required by FRCP 26(e)—the Grigsbys pivoted their theory of the case (offering no evidence or argument that Cajun developed new products, which the District Court treated as a waiver), arguing that Cajun had developed new "construction processes" that led to the final products.

This mid-litigation pivot triggered a two-fold legal defeat encompassing both procedural sanctions under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and substantive disqualification under the Internal Revenue Code. First, under FRCP 26(e)(1), a party who has responded to an interrogatory is under a mandatory, continuing duty to supplement or correct its disclosure or response in a timely manner if the party learns that the response is incomplete or incorrect in some material respect. Under FRCP 37(c)(1), "[i]f a party fails to provide information or identify a witness as required by Rule 26(a) or (e), the party is not allowed to use that information or witness to supply evidence on a motion, at a hearing, or at a trial, unless the failure was substantially justified or is harmless." Reviewing the District Court's evidentiary exclusion for abuse of discretion, the Fifth Circuit held that the District Court properly barred the Grigsbys' undisclosed "construction processes" theory under Rule 37(c)(1). Applying the four-factor test (the importance of the evidence, the prejudice to the opposing party, the possibility of curing that prejudice through a continuance, and the explanation for the failure to disclose), the courts found the change highly prejudicial because the Government had focused its summary judgment evidence and argument exclusively on the "product" theory stated in the interrogatory responses and was deprived of the opportunity to investigate the new claim; that a continuance would disturb a trial set about one month away in a case more than three years old; and that the Grigsbys offered no explanation for the change.

Second, attempting to salvage their claim on appeal, the Grigsbys argued that their construction processes were inherently intertwined with and led to the final physical product, such that identifying the product should encompass the underlying construction processes. The Fifth Circuit held that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in excluding the argument and, in rejecting the claimed products, explained that while Cajun's construction processes may have led to the final product, the Internal Revenue Code requires each business component to be evaluated separately. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the qualification tests of § 41(d)(1) "shall be applied separately with respect to each business component of the taxpayer." Even more specifically, Congress enacted the "Special rule for production processes" in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), which mandates that "[a]ny plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component shall be treated as a separate business component (and not as part of the business component being produced)." Relying on these statutory provisions (and, in the District Court's analysis, on 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(1), which treats a product and its production process as separate business components, and on the rule against superfluities), the courts treated a construction process and the physical structure being constructed as distinct business components that must be separately identified and substantiated; the Fifth Circuit's only citation to CQ, Inc. v. TXU Mining Co., L.P., 565 F.3d 268, 277 (5th Cir. 2009), a non-tax case, was for the abuse-of-discretion standard of review that governs Rule 37 exclusions. Because the Grigsbys failed to create a genuine dispute that the four physical products were qualifying business components of Cajun, and were procedurally barred from pivoting to construction processes, their claim collapsed as a matter of law.
Substantive Technical and Contemporaneous Documentation Deficiencies

Crucially, the Fifth Circuit did not rest its business component holding solely on FRCP 37 procedural preclusion; it also evaluated the substantive evidentiary record and found it wholly deficient. Even if the "construction processes" argument had been timely disclosed during discovery, the Grigsbys failed to identify a single specific construction process or technique that was actually new or improved.

Instead of producing granular, contemporaneous engineering documentation demonstrating how specific construction processes resolved objective technological uncertainties through a structured process of experimentation, the Grigsbys offered only sweeping, conclusory assertions that Cajun "performed engineering analyses that fundamentally relied on engineering principles" during the projects. Neither the Fifth Circuit nor the District Court reached whether routine engineering activities of this kind could constitute qualified research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1); the District Court held that vague and conclusory statements cannot create a genuine issue of fact, that it would not speculate or develop arguments on a party's behalf, and that the taxpayers' obfuscation left it without any meaningful criteria to measure whether the alleged construction processes were new or improved.

This evidentiary failure aligns Grigsby with a formidable wave of modern federal appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence enforcing strict substantiation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d). In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the Seventh Circuit held that "shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice" to prove the "substantially all" (80 percent) process of experimentation test, requiring documented evidence of time and resources spent on genuine scientific or engineering experimentation rather than routine production or trial-and-error. Similarly, in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, the U.S. Tax Court rejected uncorroborated testimony and retrospective time estimates where engineering firms failed to maintain contemporaneous records establishing objective technological uncertainty and an iterative process of evaluating alternatives. In Grigsby, Cajun's failure to identify even one specific new or improved construction process left the courts to guess what processes were at issue and rendered its claim unsubstantiated at summary judgment.
The Funded Research Exclusion — Prong One: Divestiture of Substantial Rights Through Boilerplate IP, Confidentiality, and FAR Clauses

Although the failure to establish a qualifying business component was sufficient by itself to affirm summary judgment, the Fifth Circuit proceeded to analyze the alternative ground of the "funded research" exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d), delivering a holding of immense practical consequence for government and commercial contractors.

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), if a taxpayer performs research on behalf of another person and retains no "substantial rights" in the research under the governing agreement, the research is treated as funded and is categorically ineligible for the Section 41 credit, regardless of whether payment was contingent on success. In determining whether substantial rights are retained, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) directs the court to examine "[a]ll agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons."

The landmark federal precedent governing substantial rights is Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), which established that a researcher does not need to retain exclusive ownership of the intellectual property to possess substantial rights; rather, a researcher retains substantial rights if it maintains the right to use and commercially exploit the results of the research in its own business without having to pay the customer for that right. Conversely, as subsequent decisions in Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), and Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1, demonstrated, where commercial or government contracts contain work-for-hire, intellectual property assignment, or non-disclosure provisions that divest the contractor of title to its technical innovations or prohibit the contractor from reusing the developed information without customer consent, the contractor retains no substantial rights.

Applying this analytical framework, the Fifth Circuit examined the express contractual terms of the Methanex, Chevron, and Claiborne projects and held that Cajun had contractually surrendered all substantial rights in each instance. In the Methanex Project, Cajun's subcontract with Jacobs Field Services broadly defined "Work Product" to encompass all technical documentation, drawings, specifications, and any other technical manifestation of Cajun's efforts performed under the subcontract. The contract explicitly designated all such Work Product as "works made for hire" and vested all right, title, and interest in and to the Work Product exclusively in the ultimate client, Methanex USA. By executing a blanket work-for-hire transfer covering all technical manifestations of its work, Cajun stripped itself of any legal right to claim ownership over whatever undefined research occurred on the site.

Similarly, in the Chevron Project, Cajun's contract with Chevron Products Company contained an expansive intellectual property and confidentiality clause governing "Technical Information." The contract defined "Technical Information" to include "all inventions, discoveries or improvements (patentable or otherwise) that are made or conceived by [Cajun] in performing the Work and all patent rights associated with these inventions, discoveries or improvements." Under the agreement, Cajun agreed that all inventions, discoveries, and improvements made or conceived in performing the Services (and all patent rights based on them) belong to Chevron or an Affiliate designated by Chevron, that all drawings, documents, engineering and other data prepared by Cajun were Chevron's work for hire and Chevron's property from the time of preparation (Section 2.20.3, on which the Fifth Circuit also relied), that Cajun would promptly disclose all such inventions or improvements to Chevron and assign any resulting patent applications to the designated Affiliate, and that all Technical Information would be "used only for performance of the Services for [Chevron]." Furthermore, Cajun was prohibited from disclosing Technical Information to any third party without Chevron's express written consent, agreed that Chevron was entitled to immediate equitable relief, including a restraining order and preliminary injunction, upon any breach or threatened breach, and agreed that these restrictive covenants remained in full force even after the Chevron Project concluded.

In the Claiborne Project, Cajun's flood-control contract with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers incorporated standard Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) clauses, specifically FAR § 52.232-5(f), codified at 48 C.F.R. § 52.232-5(f) ("Payments under Fixed-Price Construction Contracts"). Under FAR § 52.232-5(f), "[a]ll material and work covered by progress payments made shall, at the time of payment, become the sole property of the Government." Because "work" is defined under the applicable 2011 version of FAR 2.101 to mean construction activity (including structures and improvements of all types), and any new or improved method of construction is logically part of Cajun's construction activity, title to all work covered by progress payments vested in the United States Government; the Grigsbys never addressed how Cajun could have retained substantial rights in its methods of construction, which the District Court treated as a tacit admission that they could not overcome the transfer-of-title provision.

Confronted with these unambiguous contractual provisions, the Grigsbys argued that Cajun nonetheless retained substantial rights because nothing in the contracts precluded Cajun from performing the same types of activities and using the same means and methods on other projects; the Fifth Circuit noted that they gave no specific examples of these means and methods, leaving the courts to guess what Cajun could bring to future projects aside from additional experience in its field. The Fifth Circuit squarely rejected this argument. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), "incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research." As Judge Higginbotham concluded, quoting Tangel v. Commissioner, after Cajun assigned away all rights to the work developed during the Methanex, Chevron, and Claiborne projects, "it is hard to see what rights—much less what substantial rights" Cajun retained in its undefined research.
The Funded Research Exclusion — Prong Two: Rebuttal of the Fixed-Price Risk Presumption Under Payment Contingency Analysis

The fourth representative project—the East Bank Project with the Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans—presented a distinct legal configuration because the contract contained no provisions addressing the ownership of work product, intellectual property, or research developed during the project. Because the contract did not strip Cajun of substantial rights on its face, the Fifth Circuit turned to the other conjunctive requirement of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1): whether the amounts payable to Cajun were contingent on the success of the research.

As the Fifth Circuit explained, quoting Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868, 870 (Fed. Cir. 1995), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d) (formerly § 1.41-5, redesignated in 2001 by Credit for Increasing Research Activities, 66 Fed. Reg. 280, 295 (2001)) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e) operate as "mirror image" rules designed to determine whether the contractor or the customer bears the financial risk of the research. Under § 1.41-4A(d)(1), "amounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2)) are not treated as funding." Under § 1.41-2(e)(2), an expense is paid for the product or result of research only if the payment is contingent on the success of the research, meaning the contractor is paid only if the research succeeds in producing the desired technical output.

In federal R&D tax credit litigation—rooted in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), and Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015)—fixed-price contracts are more likely to be deemed unfunded because the researcher bears the financial risk of failure, and authority cited by the District Court (Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner) presumes them to be unfunded with respect to payment contingency, although the Fifth Circuit stressed that Fairchild and Geosyntec do not stand for the proposition that all fixed-price contracts are per se unfunded (Geosyntec itself found the contracts at issue funded). The rationale is that under a true fixed-price contract, the contractor must deliver a functioning, specification-compliant product or result for a set price; if the contractor's technical design fails, the contractor must absorb the financial cost of re-engineering and fixing the defective work at its own expense, or forfeit payment upon customer rejection.

The Grigsbys advanced three arguments that the East Bank Project was unfunded: first, relying on 26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-4A(d) and 1.41-2(e), that payment was contingent upon Cajun delivering a "result or product"; second, that they were entitled to the credit simply because SWBNO, the payor, was not; and third, that the fixed-price project was "inherently risky." However, the Fifth Circuit held that the first argument improperly conflated amounts payable that are contingent on the success of the research with contracts for products or services (the taxpayers admitted that none of Cajun's payment was for merely conducting research), that the regulations do not require the credit to be allocated to someone in every contract, and that a contract's label as "fixed-price" is not talismanic; courts must scrutinize the actual payment, indemnification, and risk-allocation clauses within the four corners of the agreement.

Upon inspecting the East Bank contract, the District Court held that its express terms definitively rebutted the fixed-price risk presumption, and the Fifth Circuit agreed that, even if the regulations allocate the credit to the party bearing the risk of unsuccessful research, Cajun was compensated for all risks associated with the project. First, the East Bank contract's "Monthly Payments" provision expressly stipulated that the payments made to Cajun compensated it for "all loss, damages or risks of every description, connected with or resulting from the nature of the work, or from any obstructions or difficulties encountered, of any sort or nature whatsoever". Rather than forcing Cajun to absorb the financial loss of unexpected technical obstacles or failed experimental methodologies, the contract guaranteed compensation for all risks, obstructions, and difficulties encountered during performance. Second, as the District Court noted, the East Bank contract provided that if SWBNO's Engineer determined that laboratory inspection and testing was required, the client (the Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans), rather than Cajun, would pay its cost, with Cajun bearing no part of it; the Fifth Circuit added a further, independent ground: Cajun's Form 6765 claimed the credit entirely for wages, yet the contract compensated Cajun for all general foremen, foremen, labor, and teams at the rates actually paid, plus a fee for superintendence, general expense, and profit, so the claimed wages were funded under any plain meaning of the term.

Because the East Bank contract insulated Cajun from the financial fallout of technical difficulties and shifted the direct cost of laboratory testing onto the municipal customer, Cajun bore no genuine economic risk that its compensation would be forfeited if a research effort failed. Consequently, payments under the East Bank contract were not contingent on the success of research under 26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-4A(d)(1) and 1.41-2(e)(2), rendering the project "funded" and ineligible for the credit under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and procedural requirement adjudicated in Grigsby v. United States against the specific legal or evidentiary deficiency committed by the taxpayer and the controlling standard of proof enforced by the Fifth Circuit.

headers: Fifth Circuit's Controlling Standard of Proof

cells: 1. Presumption of Correctness & Summary Judgment Burden
26 U.S.C. §§ 41, 6532(b), 7405; 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d); FRCP 56; Carson v. United States, 560 F.2d 693 (5th Cir. 1977); Sealy Power, Ltd. v. Comm'r, 46 F.3d 382 (5th Cir. 1995)

Argued that the District Court improperly placed the summary judgment burden on them as non-movants and that the IRS determination was insufficient because it did not result from an administrative proceeding, attempting to shift the summary judgment burden to the Government without producing affirmative, usable substantiation records.

Tax credits are narrowly construed matters of legislative grace. An IRS disallowance letter carries a "presumption of correctness." Once the presumption attaches, the taxpayer must produce competent, specific evidence rebutting it and substantiating every statutory element of § 41 (the Government retains the ultimate burden of showing that a refund was erroneous, and here also met its own burden of production).
2. Discovery Consistency & Duty to Supplement
FRCP 26(a), FRCP 26(e), and FRCP 37(c)(1)

Swore in verified interrogatory responses that Cajun developed a new "product" on each representative project, then pivoted in summary judgment opposition to claiming "construction processes" without ever supplementing discovery under Rule 26(e).

Under FRCP 37(c)(1), a party that fails to timely supplement interrogatory responses under Rule 26(e) is strictly barred from using undisclosed legal theories or factual assertions to oppose summary judgment unless the failure is substantially justified or harmless.
3. Business Component Identification & Separate Evaluation
26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), § 41(d)(2)(A), § 41(d)(2)(B), and § 41(d)(2)(C) (Special Rule for Production Processes); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(1)

Claimed client-owned physical structures (described by the Fifth Circuit as two oil refineries and two flood control systems) as "products" of Cajun, and argued on appeal that construction processes should be evaluated as part of the final product.

Under § 41(d)(2)(A) and (C), courts must evaluate each business component separately. A construction or production process is a distinct statutory business component from the physical product being constructed and cannot be conflated with the final deliverable.
4. Technological Uncertainty, Experimentation & Substantiation

Failed to identify a single specific new or improved construction process or product; offered only vague assertions that Cajun "performed engineering analyses that fundamentally relied on engineering principles" using standard industry methods.

Vague, conclusory statements cannot defeat summary judgment. Taxpayers must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d)) to substantiate the credit and must specifically identify each new or improved business component; neither court reached the process-of-experimentation test.
5. Funded Research Exclusion: Substantial Rights Prong (Commercial Contracts)
26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(3); Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000); Tangel v. Comm'r, T.C. Memo. 2021-1

Executed the Methanex subcontract designating all "Work Product" as "works made for hire" owned by Methanex USA, and the Chevron contract assigning all "Technical Information" (inventions, discoveries, improvements, patent rights) to Chevron with perpetual non-use and confidentiality restrictions.

All agreements must be examined under § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Boilerplate work-for-hire, IP assignment, and surviving non-disclosure/exclusive-use clauses divest the researcher of substantial rights. Incidental benefits (general know-how or experience) do not satisfy § 1.41-4A(d)(2).
6. Funded Research Exclusion: Substantial Rights Prong (Federal Contracts)

Executed the Claiborne U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contract incorporating FAR § 52.232-5(f) thereby vesting sole ownership of "all material and work" covered by progress payments in the U.S. Government, and offered no explanation of how Cajun retained rights in its methods of construction.

Where an incorporated FAR progress payment provision transfers sole title in all "material and work" (with "work" defined broadly as construction activity) to the federal government and the taxpayer cannot explain how it retained rights in its methods of construction, the contractor retains no substantial rights.
7. Funded Research Exclusion: Payment Contingency / Economic Risk Prong

26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); 26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-4A(d)(1) & 1.41-2(e)(2); Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995); Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015)

Relied on the "fixed-price" label of the East Bank contract while ignoring its "Monthly Payments" clause (which compensated Cajun for "all loss, damages or risks of every description" and "any obstructions or difficulties encountered") and client-paid lab testing provisions.

While fixed-price contracts are more likely to be deemed unfunded (but are not per se unfunded), specific contractual terms shifting the financial risk of technical difficulties, losses, or laboratory testing onto the client rebut that presumption. If the contractor is insulated from financial loss upon research failure, or is fully compensated for the very wages it claims as research expenses, the work is funded.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the holdings of Grigsby v. United States into actionable tax and legal compliance protocols, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic commercial and government engineering projects confronting the exact statutory, procedural, and contractual pitfalls adjudicated by the Fifth Circuit. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, contract terms, technical documentation, and experimentation tracking to overcome the court's objections and satisfy all requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41.
Case Study 1: Industrial EPC Contractor Executing a Petrochemical Plant Relocation and Deep-Soil Stabilization Subcontract
Baseline Scenario and Inherent Grigsby Pitfalls

Apex Gulf Industrial, Inc. ("Apex"), a domestic S corporation heavy civil and industrial engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractor based in Houston, Texas, is awarded a $42 million capped subcontract by a prime EPC contractor ("PrimeCo") on behalf of an international chemical manufacturer ("ChemCorp"). The project involves relocating an ammonia synthesis train to coastal Louisiana, requiring Apex to design and execute a novel deep-soil stabilization and modular foundation system capable of supporting extreme dynamic compressor loads in highly compressible deltaic clay.

In its unmediated baseline posture, Apex faces four fatal Grigsby pitfalls. First, Apex's accounting department tracks all project costs under a single macro job code ("Job 24-105: ChemCorp Ammonia Foundation") and intends to list the "Ammonia Plant Foundation System" (a physical product delivered to ChemCorp) as the business component on its tax return and in potential audit interrogatories, replicating Cajun's conflation of products and processes under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2). Second, replicating the Methanex subcontract failure in Grigsby, Section 14.1 of PrimeCo's standard subcontract states that all "Work Product," including all drawings, specifications, calculations, technical data, and any other technical manifestation of Subcontractor's efforts, shall be deemed "works made for hire" and all right, title, and interest therein shall vest exclusively in ChemCorp upon creation. Third, mirroring the Chevron contract failure in Grigsby, Section 14.2 of the subcontract defines "Technical Information" to include all inventions, discoveries, or improvements (patentable or otherwise) conceived or made by Subcontractor in performing the Work, and restricts Apex to using such Technical Information solely for the performance of Services for ChemCorp, prohibiting post-completion disclosure or reuse on third-party projects without ChemCorp's prior written consent. Fourth, Apex relies on year-end interviews conducted by an outside tax credit consultant in which project managers generally state that they "performed geotechnical engineering analyses relying on soil mechanics principles," suffering from the exact lack of specificity condemned by the Fifth Circuit.
Step 1: Project Governance and Business Component Segregation Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) and (C)

To avoid the procedural trap of FRCP 26(e) and 37(c)(1) and the substantive bar of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), Apex establishes a Pre-Construction Tax and Technical Governance Committee prior to project mobilization. The governance committee formally prohibits classifying the physical ammonia plant foundation as a "product" business component of Apex, recognizing that the physical real property improvement belongs to ChemCorp and is not held for sale, lease, or license by Apex in its own trade or business.

Instead, applying the special rule for production processes under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) and the Fifth Circuit's requirement in Grigsby that each business component be evaluated separately, Apex formally charters two specific, separate internal business components before engineering commences. The first chartered component is designated as Business Component 24-105-P1 (Process), defined as a proprietary Automated Multi-Stage Colloidal Silica and Polyurethane Grout Injection Process designed to achieve uniform shear-modulus stiffening in high-plasticity marine clays without inducing hydraulic heave. The second chartered component is designated as Business Component 24-105-T1 (Technique/Machinery), defined as a Vibro-Acoustic Resonance Damping Piling Technique utilizing a custom-fabricated variable-eccentricity hydraulic vibratory hammer head to drive hollow-core steel piles within 15 feet of live petrochemical pipelines without exceeding peak particle velocity (PPV) thresholds of 0.2 inches per second. By locking in these specific "process" and "technique" business components in contemporaneous corporate records, Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) disclosures, and initial audit presentations, Apex ensures total consistency between administrative tax filings and any subsequent FRCP 26 discovery responses, eliminating the risk of a Grigsby Rule 37(c)(1) preclusion sanction.
Step 2: Contractual Restructuring to Preserve Substantial Rights Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)

Before executing the subcontract with PrimeCo, Apex's legal counsel and tax advisors negotiate targeted redlines to Sections 14.1 and 14.2 to satisfy the substantial rights standard of Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States and overcome the Methanex and Chevron holdings in Grigsby. Specifically, Apex bifurcates "Site-Specific Deliverable Work Product" from "Contractor Process IP," amending Section 14.1 so that the "work made for hire" transfer applies strictly to the tangible physical structure and the final as-built architectural and structural blueprints specific to ChemCorp's Geismar facility layout.

Simultaneously, Apex inserts an explicit Intellectual Property Reservation and License-Back Clause into Section 14.2. This revised contractual provision stipulates that notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the subcontract or any incorporated Prime Contract documents, "Work Product" and "Technical Information" transferred to the Owner or Prime Contractor shall not include Subcontractor's underlying engineering methodologies, construction processes, geotechnical stabilization techniques, chemical grout formulations, equipment modifications, software algorithms, or analytical models conceived, developed, or refined by Subcontractor during the performance of the Work ("Subcontractor Process IP"). The clause further establishes that Subcontractor shall retain sole ownership of—or at a minimum an irrevocable, perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive right and license to use, reproduce, modify, patent, and commercially exploit—all Subcontractor Process IP for any other client or in any future project in Subcontractor's trade or business, without seeking consent from, or paying any royalty or fee to, Prime Contractor or Owner. Finally, the clause narrows the surviving confidentiality obligations so that they apply strictly to ChemCorp's proprietary chemical manufacturing formulas and facility security layouts, rather than restricting Apex's commercial reuse of its own construction processes.

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), which mandates reviewing all agreements entered into between the researcher and third parties, this explicit contractual reservation neutralizes both the Methanex work-for-hire trap and the Chevron perpetual non-use restriction. Even if ChemCorp receives a concurrent license to operate and maintain its physical foundation, Apex retains the unfettered legal right to use its newly developed grouting process and vibratory damping technique on future third-party jobs without paying for that right, fully satisfying Lockheed Martin and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) with respect to substantial rights; because a capped subcontract typically reimburses billed labor and costs (as the Methanex subcontract did), however, Apex must still separately satisfy the payment-contingency prong, since the Fifth Circuit in Grigsby (citing Example 1 of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A) noted that a researcher wholly compensated for its otherwise qualified expenditures is not entitled to the credit notwithstanding any rights retained in the research.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation Protocol Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d)

To satisfy the recordkeeping mandate of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) and avoid the vague, retrospective assertions rejected in Grigsby, Betz, and Phoenix Design Group, Apex implements a bifurcated Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) in its enterprise resource planning (ERP) and timekeeping systems. Under this accounting protocol, routine site grading, excavation, rebar tying, and standard concrete pouring are billed to non-qualifying construction cost codes (24-105-CONST-001) and excluded from QRE calculations. Conversely, time and supplies expended by geotechnical engineers, materials scientists, and field test technicians working directly on the two chartered business components are contemporaneously recorded to dedicated R&D sub-codes (24-105-RD-P1 for the grouting process and 24-105-RD-T1 for the vibro-acoustic technique).

Furthermore, Apex enforces a mandatory digital substantiation rule requiring each weekly timecard entry billed to an R&D sub-code to be linked in the ERP system to a contemporaneous technical artifact. These linked records include dated finite element analysis (FEA) simulation files, rheometer viscosity test logs, field piezometer pressure readouts, and engineering change notices (ECNs), thereby establishing an audit-ready, contemporaneous nexus between employee wages or supply costs and the specific business component under development.
Step 4: Structured Process of Experimentation Tracking Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C)

To prove that "substantially all" (80 percent or more) of the activities within 24-105-RD-P1 and 24-105-RD-T1 constitute elements of a process of experimentation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Little Sandy Coal, Apex maintains a formal, four-stage scientific method log for each business component. In the first stage, the log documents the objective technological uncertainty by recording why standard industry grouting methods—such as ordinary Portland cement jet grouting—cannot achieve the required 1,500 kPa unconfined compressive strength in deltaic clay without fracturing adjacent soil strata, establishing uncertainty regarding the appropriate design and method of the injection process. In the second stage, the engineering team records three competing chemical rheology hypotheses involving varying silica nanoparticle concentrations at 15 percent, 22 percent, and 30 percent by weight combined with delayed-catalyst polyurethane resins. In the third stage, the dossier captures 3D geotechnical PLAXIS modeling runs followed by controlled field test-cell injections equipped with real-time inclinometers and cone penetrometer testing (CPT) rigs. In the fourth stage, the project engineers formally log the evaluation of failures and design refinements, documenting that Iteration 1 (15 percent silica) failed shear-wave velocity testing at 48 hours and Iteration 2 (30 percent silica) caused premature gelation in the injection lances, which directly led to the formulation and validation of Iteration 3 (22 percent silica with a dual-stage thermal retardant catalyst).
Case Study 2: Civil Infrastructure Contractor Executing a Joint Federal-Municipal Flood-Control Culvert and Pumping System
Baseline Scenario and Inherent Grigsby Pitfalls

Delta Heavy Civil, LLC ("Delta"), a domestic C corporation civil infrastructure contractor based in New Orleans, Louisiana, enters into a $65 million fixed-price construction contract with a joint municipal-federal Flood Protection Authority ("Authority") co-funded by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The project requires constructing a subterranean reinforced concrete box culvert and high-capacity axial-flow storm surge pumping station beneath an urban canal.

In its baseline posture, Delta faces the exact government contracting and risk-allocation traps that disqualified the Claiborne and East Bank projects in Grigsby. First, replicating the Claiborne pitfall, the contract incorporates standard Federal Acquisition Regulation clauses by reference, including FAR § 52.232-5(f) (48 C.F.R. § 52.232-5(f)), which provides that all material and work covered by progress payments made shall, at the time of payment, become the sole property of the Government. No special contract clause distinguishes physical construction materials from Delta's underlying research and engineering techniques. Second, replicating the East Bank pitfall, although the contract is labeled "Fixed-Price," Section 9.4 ("Monthly Progress Payments and Site Risks") states that monthly payments compensate Delta for "all loss, damages or risks of every description, connected with or resulting from the nature of the work, or from any obstructions or difficulties encountered, of any sort or nature whatsoever." Additionally, Section 11.2 states that the Authority will directly reimburse Delta outside the fixed price for all third-party hydraulic flume testing and concrete materials laboratory testing. Third, Delta's tax preparer assumes that because the contract header says "Firm Fixed-Price," the contract is automatically unfunded under Fairchild Industries without reading the underlying payment and FAR clauses.
Step 1: Project Governance and Pre-Bid Contract Review Protocol

As emphasized by legal commentators following Grigsby, contracting officers and corporate estimators must confer with R&D tax counsel prior to bid submission and contract execution to prevent boilerplate clauses from sacrificing research credits. To institutionalize this safeguard, Delta implements a corporate governance mandate requiring any public works or commercial contract exceeding $5 million to undergo a two-prong Funded Research Matrix Review—evaluating both 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) payment contingency and § 1.41-4A(d)(2) substantial rights—during the pre-award bid clarification and contract negotiation window.

Concurrently, prior to site mobilization, Delta's engineering governance board charters two distinct process and technique business components under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) so that its tax claim is never tied to the physical municipal canal culvert. The first chartered component is designated as Business Component FP-01 (Construction Process), consisting of a Cryogenic Freeze-Wall and Pressurized Slurry Micro-Tunneling Process for excavating box culvert sections through water-bearing pleistocene sand layers beneath active urban levees without inducing differential settlement. The second chartered component is designated as Business Component FP-02 (Engineering Technique), consisting of an Anti-Cavitation Vortex-Suppressing Intake Baffle Assembly Technique developed to eliminate destructive harmonic cavitation in high-volume storm surge pumps operating under variable head pressures.
Step 2: Contractual Restructuring to Overcome the Claiborne (FAR) and East Bank (Payment Contingency) Pitfalls
To prevent disqualification under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), Delta executes two critical contractual modifications via a bilateral Pre-Award Addendum and Special Contract Requirement (Section H).

First, to neutralize the Claiborne FAR § 52.232-5(f) title transfer trap under the substantial rights prong, Delta leverages FAR Part 27 (Patents, Data, and Copyrights), which authorizes federal procuring agencies to define intellectual property and technical data rights separately from physical construction materials even when mandatory fixed-price construction payment clauses apply. Delta negotiates a Special Contract Requirement (Clause H.12) clarifying the scope of FAR § 52.232-5(f) and incorporating FAR § 52.227-11 (Patent Rights—Ownership by the Contractor) and FAR § 52.227-14 (Rights in Data—General) principles. Clause H.12 expressly states that the vesting of title to "all material and work covered by progress payments" under FAR § 52.232-5(f) applies strictly to tangible construction materials, physical equipment incorporated into the permanent structure, and physical construction-in-progress at the project site. The clause further provides that nothing in FAR § 52.232-5(f) or the Contract shall divest the Contractor of ownership or substantial rights in any new or improved construction processes, dewatering or ground-freezing techniques, hydraulic modeling methods, or engineering inventions ("Contractor Research Processes") developed by the Contractor during performance, and that while the Government and Authority receive a non-exclusive license to operate and maintain the completed physical flood-control facility, the Contractor retains title to and the unconditional right to use, license, and commercially exploit all Contractor Research Processes in its trade or business without payment or obligation to the Government or Authority. This provision directly resolves the Claiborne failure identified by the Fifth Circuit by establishing that progress payments purchase only physical materials and facility deliverables, leaving substantial rights in the research processes vested in Delta under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).

Second, to re-establish true economic risk and payment contingency under 26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-4A(d)(1) and 1.41-2(e)(2) and overcome the East Bank pitfall, Delta strikes the risk-insulating indemnification wording in Section 9.4 and the testing reimbursement in Section 11.2, replacing them with strict performance-contingent risk provisions aligned with Fairchild Industries and Geosyntec Consultants. Specifically, Section 9.4 is revised to state that the Contractor's Fixed Price is inclusive of all technical and engineering risks, and that monthly progress payments constitute provisional financing advances only and shall not compensate the Contractor for losses, damages, or technical failures resulting from experimental construction methods or engineering designs. A companion clause, Section 9.5, is added to stipulate that all provisional monthly progress payments are strictly contingent upon the final technical success and formal acceptance of the completed work in accordance with the hydraulic and structural performance specifications of the contract; in the event any construction process, freeze-wall stabilization method, or hydraulic intake design fails to meet performance specifications, the Contractor must, at its sole cost and expense without adjustment to the Fixed Price, re-engineer, demolish, reconstruct, and re-test the failed work, or refund all progress payments attributable to the non-conforming work upon rejection by the Authority. Finally, Section 11.2 is amended to mandate that the Contractor shall bear 100 percent of the financial cost of all computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling, physical scale-model hydraulic flume testing, and geotechnical freeze-core laboratory testing required to develop and validate its construction processes and intake designs, with no separate reimbursement from the Authority.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation and Cost Segregation Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d)

To ensure that only eligible expenses tied to the two process business components are claimed, Delta implements a rigorous cost-segregation and documentation architecture. Even assuming the modified contract is treated as unfunded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) (which also requires that Delta's compensation not be structured as payment for the very labor it claims as QREs, the further ground on which the Fifth Circuit held the East Bank Project funded), Delta does not claim the entire $65 million contract value; all standard pile driving, sheet-pile installation, concrete forming, and commercial pump procurement are isolated in non-QRE construction accounts.

Delta captures only the W-2 wages of its hydraulic engineers, geotechnical specialists, and CAD/CFD modelers (under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)), disposable cryogenic sensor arrays and scale-flume fabrication supplies (under § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), and 65 percent of third-party university hydraulic laboratory testing invoices (as qualified contract research expenses under § 41(b)(3)) strictly within dedicated R&D sub-ledgers FP-01-EXP and FP-02-EXP. Each time entry requires a contemporaneous daily technical narrative describing the exact experimental activity performed and linking the labor hours to the corresponding test protocol.
Step 4: Structured Process of Experimentation Tracking Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C)

Delta compiles a contemporaneous Research and Experimentation Technical Dossier for both FP-01 and FP-02 to prove compliance with the four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1). For Business Component FP-01 (Cryogenic Freeze-Wall Process), the dossier preserves baseline hydrogeological data showing brackish groundwater flow velocities of 4.2 feet per day, which exceeds the 3.0 feet per day thermal dissipation limit of standard liquid brine freeze pipes, thereby establishing objective technological uncertainty. The dossier logs 14 iterative thermal-fluid coupled finite element modeling runs comparing liquid nitrogen dual-conduit spacing configurations, followed by field test-pit instrumentation logs where thermocouple arrays measured ice-wall closure rates, documenting an unsuccessful initial spacing configuration (which left an unfrozen thermal window) and the subsequent successful redesign utilizing staggered directional freeze lances.

For Business Component FP-02 (Anti-Cavitation Intake Technique), the dossier archives Ansys Fluent 3D computational fluid dynamics (CFD) turbulence simulations alongside video and pressure-transducer logs from a 1:10 Froude-scale physical acrylic flume model. The records trace five distinct geometric iterations of the floor-splitter cone and sidewall baffle angles until sub-surface vortex formation was eliminated across all operational pump speeds, providing contemporaneous evidence of a scientific process of experimentation that addresses the specificity and substantiation deficiencies identified by the courts in Grigsby.
Synthesis of Remedial Governance Versus Disqualified Practices
The table below synthesizes the operational transformation achieved in Case Studies 1 and 2 compared against the disqualified practices in Grigsby v. United States.

headers: Disqualified Practice in Grigsby v. United States

cells: Business Component Definition (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2))
Identified client-owned physical structures ("products") in discovery, then attempted an unannounced summary judgment pivot to undefined "construction processes."
Defines discrete, proprietary construction processes and engineering techniques under § 41(d)(2)(C) prior to mobilization, maintaining strict consistency across tax filings and FRCP 26 disclosures.
Commercial IP & Work-for-Hire Clauses (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2))

Accepted boilerplate clauses making all "Work Product" a "work made for hire" (Methanex) and assigning all "Technical Information" and inventions to the client with perpetual non-use covenants (Chevron).

Bifurcates site-specific physical deliverables from "Contractor Process IP," carving out construction methodologies from work-for-hire clauses and securing a perpetual, royalty-free right to exploit all processes on future projects.
Federal Procurement FAR Clauses (48 C.F.R. § 52.232-5(f))
Allowed FAR § 52.232-5(f) to transfer sole ownership of "all material and work" covered by progress payments to the U.S. Government without reservation (Claiborne).

Incorporates Special Contract Requirements (Section H / FAR Part 27) restricting FAR § 52.232-5(f) title transfer to tangible construction materials while reserving contractor ownership and exploitation rights in research processes.
Economic Risk & Payment Contingency (26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-4A(d)(1) & 1.41-2(e)(2))

Relied on a "fixed-price" label while the contract's "Monthly Payments" clause provided full compensation to Cajun for "all loss, damages or risks" and shifted lab testing costs to the client (East Bank).

Eliminates loss/obstacle indemnification, makes interim payments provisional advances subject to full clawback until technical acceptance testing succeeds (Fairchild Industries), and allocates all prototype/lab testing costs to the contractor.
Technical Substantiation & Recordkeeping (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d))
Relied on a retroactive consulting study sampling 105 projects and offered only vague assertions that Cajun "performed engineering analyses that fundamentally relied on engineering principles."
Deploys sub-ledger WBS cost codes tied directly to each process business component, supported by contemporaneous daily time narratives, FEA/CFD models, failed test iterations, and laboratory logs.

metaDescription: Grigsby v. United States, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), is a key federal R&D tax credit case for construction contractors claiming Section 41 credits.
